Deliverable 7.4.1: Report quantifying the difference in performance between model-based and model-free control in the presence of faults The report for Deliverable 7.4.1 as originally submitted is appended. The report summarizes two American Control Conference 2024 papers from Oregon State University addressing biofouling impacts on marine energy systems and control-based mitigation strategies. The first paper (Skrovanek & Brekken) uses WEC-Sim to model how biofouling-induced drag affects the RM3 point absorber, finding that at H=2m and the resonant period of 12 seconds, PTO power decreases by 15% and peak velocity/displacement decrease by 10% when roughness increases from zero to 0.1m. Importantly, the study shows that optimal damping control can recover 5–10% of the lost power, demonstrating that adaptive control tuning can partially compensate for biofouling effects without physical cleaning. The second paper (Barton, Brekken, Cao) applies reinforcement learning to marine hydrokinetic turbines, using a SARSA algorithm with Gaussian RBF features to adaptively adjust damping coefficients as biofouling shifts the Cp(λ) curve. In a Mississippi River case study, the RL controller outperformed a fixed non-adaptive controller by nearly 1% annually, approaching the performance of perfect biofouling compensation. The deliverable also includes extended work from Sam Barton's MS thesis on life-extending control for HKT power electronics, which are identified as weak points due to thermal cycling failures. This work uses a monetary-based reward function balancing energy revenue against converter replacement costs, with an RL agent adjusting the feedback torque gain k to optimize the tradeoff. Case studies using real tidal flow and LMP pricing data from 2019 and 2024 showed the RL method reduced power electronics 5 life consumption by 77–85% with energy generation impacts of 6–25%, resulting in revenue impacts ranging from -1.3% to +45.4% depending on energy prices. Deliverable 7.4.2: Submit journal or conference publication on model- mismatch and fault-tolerant control There are two main papers summarizing the Task 7 results: • D. Skrovanek and T. Brekken, “Impact of biofouling on point absorber wave energy converter performance and control,” in 2024 American Control Conference (ACC), pp. 3328–3333, 2024. • S. Barton, T. K. Brekken, and Y. Cao, “Reinforcement learning control for enhancing marine hydrokinetic turbine energy generation,” in 2024 American Control Conference (ACC), pp. 1044–1050, 2024. Those papers are appended to this report. The Skrovanek and Brekken paper investigates how biofouling affects the performance of point absorber wave energy converters using WEC-Sim simulations of the RM3 reference model. The authors develop a drag coefficient model based on experimentally-derived relationships from the literature, relating surface roughness (average biofouling protrusion k divided by characteristic dimension D) to drag coefficient Cd. While existing models were developed for flow perpendicular to cylinders, the authors apply the percent increase in drag to the axial flow case relevant to heaving WECs. The drag force is modeled as proportional to the square of velocity, and the study examines how this nonlinear effect impacts WEC dynamics by sweeping wave heights from 1–4 m, periods from 4–16 s, and biofouling protrusion from 0 to 0.1 m.
